claims.text: Conventionally processed equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi has a relatively coarse, homogeneous microstructure without significant nanoscale precipitates.
High-strain cold rolling followed by short-duration annealing at 600–700°C can produce partial recrystallization while preserving ultrafine grains.
The proposed processing treatment will generate nanoscale precipitates in equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The proposed processing treatment will generate or preserve internal twin boundaries.
Severe plastic deformation refines the grain structure and introduces strain-induced defects.
Controlled short-duration annealing facilitates nanoscale precipitation.
Controlled short-duration annealing stabilizes twin boundaries.
Ultrafine grains, nanoscale precipitates, and twin boundaries synergistically obstruct dislocation motion.
The hierarchical microstructure enhances stress transfer.
The hierarchical microstructure deflects crack propagation.
The treatment will increase yield strength by approximately 20–30% relative to a conventional coarse, homogeneous microstructure.
The treatment will retain or slightly improve ductility despite the increase in strength.
The treatment will increase Young's modulus.
The treatment will improve fracture toughness or fracture resistance.
Excessively aggressive annealing will cause complete recrystallization and loss of the hierarchical microstructure.
Loss of the hierarchical microstructure through excessive annealing will prevent the expected property improvements.
The method is applicable primarily to alloys that tolerate severe deformation and controlled annealing without adverse phase transformations.
The reproducibility and long-term stability of the engineered microstructure under operational loading are uncertain.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires improved fracture toughness, but the falsification rule accepts merely comparable fracture toughness, so a result with no toughness improvement could satisfy the stated success criterion.

A higher Young's modulus is part of the predicted outcome, but the decisive falsification rule imposes no modulus requirement; unchanged or reduced modulus would therefore not necessarily falsify the full hypothesis.
